cards.q: In Git, what is a commit?
options: A copy emailed to the team
A saved snapshot, with a message
A backup of the whole hard disk
A branch that has been deleted
cards.why: Each commit records the state of every tracked file, who made it and why, so you can go back or compare.

cards.q: Why make a change on a branch?
options: It keeps the change apart until merged
Branches run faster than main does
Git cannot commit straight to main
It deletes the old code for you
cards.why: Main stays working while you experiment; a merge brings the change in once it is tested.

cards.q: Put the steps for sharing a change in order.
items: git push to the shared repository
cards.why: Add stages the change, commit records it locally, push sends it to the remote.

cards.q: Match each Linux command with what it does.
pairs: Lists the files in a directory
Runs a command as the administrator
cards.why: The everyday commands of the shell.

cards.q: Permissions rw-r--r-- as a three-digit octal number (read 4, write 2, execute 1)?
cards.why: Owner rw- = 4 + 2 = 6; group r-- = 4; others r-- = 4: `chmod 644`.

cards.q: What does `journalctl -u myapp` show?
options: The files myapp has open right now
myapp's source code and config files
The users who have run myapp recently
The log of the service myapp
cards.why: systemd services log to the journal; `systemctl status myapp` shows the latest lines, `journalctl -u` the lot.

cards.q: What does `len([3, 5, 7])` give in Python?
cards.why: len counts the items in a list: three.
A slice [1:3] takes indexes 1 and 2 (the end is left out): 20 + 30.

cards.q: What is `total` after this Python runs? `total = 0` then `for i in range({n}): total += i`
cards.why: range({n}) is 0 to {n} − 1; their sum is {n}({n} − 1) ÷ 2 = {answer}.

cards.q: Which SQL statement reads rows from a table?
options: INSERT
SELECT
UPDATE
DELETE
cards.why: SELECT reads; INSERT adds rows; UPDATE changes them; DELETE removes them.

cards.q: What does `SELECT * FROM alarm WHERE priority = 1 ORDER BY time DESC LIMIT 10` return?
options: The ten most recent priority-1 alarms
The ten oldest alarms of any priority
Every alarm except priority 1
The first ten alarms by priority
cards.why: WHERE filters, ORDER BY time DESC puts the newest first, LIMIT keeps ten.

cards.q: An INNER JOIN of `tag` and `reading` on `tag_id` returns what?
options: Every tag, with or without any readings
Every reading, even if its tag is missing from tag
The two tables listed one after the other
Only readings with a matching tag, joined to it
cards.why: INNER keeps the matches only; a LEFT JOIN would keep every row of the left table as well.

cards.q: What does continuous integration do?
options: Deploys to production every single hour
Merges every branch without any review
Builds and tests every push automatically
Backs up the build server each night
cards.why: Every push is built and tested, so a breaking change is caught while it is small.

cards.q: With semantic versioning, what does going from 2.3.1 to 3.0.0 tell users?
options: Only bugs were fixed
There are breaking changes
New features that change nothing old
Nothing: numbers are arbitrary
cards.why: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: major for breaking changes, minor for compatible features, patch for fixes.

cards.q: Why build a release from a tagged commit?
options: It traces the release to its exact source
Tagged commits compile a lot faster
Tags hide the code from other people
Tags delete old branches automatically
cards.why: When a site reports a fault in version 1.4.2, you can check out exactly what was shipped.

cards.q: In C#, how does assigning an int differ from assigning an object of a class?
options: Both are copied in full, whatever their type
Both share a single value in memory
Classes cannot be assigned to other variables
The int is copied; the object is shared
cards.why: Value types (int, double, struct) copy their value; reference types (class) copy the reference.

cards.q: In C#, what does `new[] { 3, 8, 1, 9, 4 }.Where(x => x > {k}).Count()` return?
cards.why: Where keeps the items passing the test, Count counts them. Over {k}: count the numbers bigger than {k}.

cards.q: Why use `List<int>` rather than the old `ArrayList`?
options: It can hold many more items than ArrayList
It sorts itself as you add items to it
It is type-safe and avoids boxing
ArrayList cannot hold numbers at all
cards.why: Generics check types at compile time and store ints directly, avoiding casts and boxing.

cards.q: What is an interface in C#?
options: A window or screen of the user interface
A contract that classes implement
A class that cannot be changed
A network connection to a PLC
cards.why: Code written against IAxis works with any class that implements IAxis: a real drive or a simulator.

cards.q: What does "prefer composition over inheritance" mean?
options: Build objects from parts they hold
Never use classes at all
Always inherit from one base class
Write everything in one big class
cards.why: A Conveyor that has a Motor and a Sensor is easier to change and test than a tower of subclasses.

cards.q: Why pass a class its dependencies (dependency injection) instead of letting it create them?
options: It makes the program run faster
The C# compiler requires it
It removes the need for interfaces
So they can be swapped, as in tests
cards.why: A class that takes an IPlc in its constructor can be given the real PLC or a fake one.

cards.q: What does `await` do in C#?
options: Blocks the thread until done
Starts a separate new process
Frees the thread while it waits
Cancels the task it is given
cards.why: The UI stays responsive during I/O because the thread is not stuck waiting.

cards.q: Why avoid calling `.Result` on a task from the WPF UI thread?
options: It returns the wrong type
It can deadlock the UI
It runs the task twice
It is slower than await
cards.why: The task may need the UI thread to finish, while .Result blocks that very thread.

cards.q: A System.Threading.Timer fires every 100 ms, but its callback sometimes takes 150 ms. What can happen?
options: Callbacks overlap on threads
The timer stops firing
The late callback is skipped
The program always crashes
cards.why: Timer callbacks run on thread-pool threads regardless of whether the last one finished, so shared data needs protecting, or the timer rescheduled after each run.

cards.q: Match each part of MVVM with its job.
pairs: The state and commands the view binds to
cards.why: The view knows the view model only through bindings, so the logic can be tested without a screen.

cards.q: What is INotifyPropertyChanged for?
options: Emailing someone when data changes
Logging every property's value
Locking a property against edits
Telling bound controls a value changed
cards.why: Raise PropertyChanged and WPF re-reads the value; without it the screen does not update.

cards.q: A background thread adds items to an ObservableCollection bound to a list. What goes wrong, and the cure?
options: Nothing: WPF marshals it to the UI thread for you
Every new item appears twice
An exception: change it on the UI thread
The list sorts itself by accident
cards.why: WPF controls belong to the UI thread; marshal the change with Dispatcher.Invoke, or enable collection synchronisation.

cards.q: Which settings must match the device when opening a serial port?
options: Only the COM port number and the device's name
Baud, data bits, parity, stop bits
The device's IP address and its subnet mask
The length of the cable and its screening
cards.why: Get one wrong and you read garbage or nothing.

cards.q: Floats are packed one after another from holding register 40001. At which zero-based address does float number {n} (counting from 1) start?
cards.why: Register 40001 is address 0. Each float takes two 16-bit registers, so float 1 starts at 0, float 2 at 2, and float {n} at 2 × ({n} − 1). (Check the device's word order too.)

cards.q: Why give a PLC socket connection read timeouts and reconnect logic?
options: Without one, a dropped link hangs the app
Timeouts make every single read much faster
The PLC maker's licence requires them
Timeouts free up a lot of the server's memory
cards.why: Networks fail. The code must notice, report and reconnect, rather than freeze.

cards.q: Put these log levels in order, least to most severe.
cards.why: Set the level per site: detailed when chasing a fault, quieter in normal running.

cards.q: Why keep a PLC's IP address and port in configuration rather than in code?
options: Configuration files run faster than code
Code cannot hold strings like addresses
It hides them from the operators
They change per site without a rebuild
cards.why: Same build, different sites: settings go in configuration.

cards.q: What is wrong with `catch (Exception) { }`?
options: It catches too few exceptions to be useful
It makes the code run slower
It hides the fault without a trace
Nothing: it keeps the program up
cards.why: Catch what you can handle; log it with context; otherwise let it rise to a handler that can.

cards.q: What is a unit test?
options: A test of the whole machine on site
An automatic test of one small piece
A manual checklist for the engineer
A test of the power supply unit
cards.why: Fast and repeatable, it runs on every build.

cards.q: Why test machine software against a simulator of the hardware?
options: It is safe, repeatable, and can fake faults
Simulators are more accurate than the hardware
Real hardware cannot be tested at all
It avoids having to write any tests
cards.why: You can test a jam, a timeout or a sensor failure a hundred times without breaking anything.

cards.q: Put the three parts of a unit test in order.
items: Arrange: set up the objects and inputs
Act: call the code under test
cards.why: Arrange, Act, Assert keeps each test short and readable.

cards.q: Which pattern fits a machine's modes (Idle, Running, Faulted) and the moves between them?
options: Singleton
Factory
Decorator
State
cards.why: Each state decides what inputs mean and which state comes next, so illegal moves cannot happen.

cards.q: What does the observer pattern do?
options: It creates objects for you
It makes a class have one instance
It notifies subscribers of changes
It wraps a class to add behaviour
cards.why: C# events are observers: the HMI subscribes to a value's changes.

cards.q: What does the command pattern give you?
options: Faster execution of every single method
Actions as objects: queue, log, undo
Automatic threading of the actions
One global instance of each action
cards.why: A move request becomes an object: it can wait in a queue, be recorded in the audit log, or be reversed.

cards.q: In clean architecture, which way do dependencies point?
options: Inwards: the outer layers depend on the core
Outwards: the core depends on the database and UI
Both ways, between every pair of layers
Downwards, from the UI through to the drivers
cards.why: The UI, database and hardware drivers depend on the core, never the other way round.

cards.q: What is the main benefit of that rule for machine software?
options: The program becomes much smaller on disk
It needs no interfaces or abstractions
It runs faster across more CPU cores
Change hardware or UI, and test the logic alone
cards.why: Swapping a drive make means a new adapter, not a rewrite of the sequence logic.

cards.q: Where does a Modbus driver belong in a clean architecture?
options: In the core, next to the business rules
In the user interface layer
Outside the core, behind its interface
Copied into every layer
cards.why: The core says what it needs (an interface); the Modbus code outside provides it.

cards.q: Match each HTTP method with its usual use in a REST API.
cards.why: The method says what to do; the URL says to what.

cards.q: Match each HTTP status code with its meaning.
cards.why: 2xx success, 4xx the client's fault, 5xx the server's.

cards.q: What does it mean that REST is stateless?
options: The server stores nothing at all, ever
Each request carries all the server needs
Requests may only read data, not write
Only one client may connect at a time
cards.why: Statelessness lets any server answer any request, which is simpler to scale and to recover.

cards.q: In JavaScript, how does `const` differ from `let`?
options: It cannot be reassigned
It runs faster than let
let cannot hold numbers
const is always global
cards.why: const stops reassignment (though an object it holds can still change).

cards.q: What does `fetch('/api/value')` return?
options: The value, straight away
A string of the page's HTML
Nothing: it only sends
A Promise of the response
cards.why: Await it (or use .then), then read the body with `await response.json()`.

cards.q: How does a web HMI show a new value without reloading the page?
options: It reloads the page every second
The server edits the HTML file on disk
It fetches it and updates the element
It opens a new window for each value
cards.why: For example `el.textContent = value` after each poll, or on a WebSocket message.

cards.q: What is time-series data?
options: A table of user accounts
Values with timestamps, per tag
The program's source code
A list of alarms and nothing else
cards.why: Historians are built to store and query huge amounts of it, fast, by time range.

cards.q: Why do historians compress data with a deadband?
options: To store only real changes and save space
To encrypt the data before it is stored
To make it load faster in a spreadsheet
To delete old alarms automatically
cards.why: Swinging-door and deadband methods keep the shape of the trend while throwing away points that add nothing.

cards.q: A tag reads {a} for {t1} minutes, then {b} for {t2} minutes. What is its time-weighted average?
cards.why: Weight each value by how long it held: a plain average of the two values ignores the time.

cards.q: Which structure finds an item by its key fastest, on average?
options: An unsorted list
A linked list
A text file
A dictionary
cards.why: A hash map looks up in about constant time, however many items; a list has to be searched.

cards.q: Binary search on {n} sorted items: about how many comparisons at most?
cards.why: Each comparison halves what is left: about $\log_2 n$. A million items take about 20.

cards.q: Match each structure with how it hands items back.
cards.why: A message queue keeps order; an undo stack returns the latest first.

cards.q: How should an application store users' passwords?
options: Plain text in a file with restricted access
Encrypted with one shared key
A salted, slow hash, like bcrypt
An MD5 hash of the password
cards.why: A slow, salted hash cannot be reversed and resists guessing even if the database leaks.

cards.q: What does TLS (the S in HTTPS) provide?
options: Faster downloads of large files
Encryption and the server's identity
A firewall between networks
Safe storage for passwords
cards.why: Without it, anyone on the network can read or alter the traffic, or pretend to be the server.

cards.q: What does the principle of least privilege mean?
options: Each account gets only what it needs
Admins get fewer rights than users
Nobody needs a password any more
Everyone shares a single account
cards.why: If a service is compromised, the damage is limited to what it could do.

cards.q: What does "deterministic" mean for a real-time system?
options: It is always quick on average, over a run
It runs on one CPU core with no other tasks
It never uses any interrupts or timers
It always responds in a guaranteed time
cards.why: Hard real-time is about the worst case, not the average.

cards.q: A 1 ms control loop's cycles are measured at {a}, {b} and {c} ms. What is the jitter (the spread), in ms?
cards.answer: MAX(a, b, c) - MIN(a, b, c)
cards.why: Jitter: how far the timing varies, largest minus smallest.

cards.q: What is priority inversion?
options: Two tasks swapping priorities on purpose
A task running its instructions backwards
A high task stuck behind a low task's lock
Interrupts left switched off for too long
cards.why: The fix is priority inheritance: the low task borrows the high priority while it holds the lock.

cards.q: In C, `PORTB |= (1 << {n});` ORs in which value?
cards.why: 1 << n shifts a 1 left n places: $2^n$. OR-ing it in sets that bit and leaves the rest.

cards.q: Why declare a variable shared with an interrupt as `volatile`?
options: So it runs faster inside the main loop code
So the compiler re-reads it every time
To store it in flash memory, not RAM
To make its value constant for the program
cards.why: Without volatile the optimiser may read it once and loop for ever on the stale copy.

cards.q: In C, `reg` holds {r} (decimal). What is `(reg >> 4) & 0x0F`?
cards.why: Shift right 4 (divide by 16, dropping the remainder), then keep the low 4 bits (the remainder after dividing by 16).
